fields.exact_text: P(both red | at least one red) = P(both red) / P(at least one red) = 0.09 / 0.51 ≈ 18%. Conditioning on the event restricts the sample space, raising the probability above the unconditional 9%.
fields.reason: Correctly gives the conditional ratio 0.09/0.51 and explains why restricting the sample space raises the answer above 9%. Rounding to 18% is appropriate. All numeric claims require the conventional uniform independent draw model recorded in the prospective anchor.

fields.exact_text: P(both red) = 0.3² = 0.09; P(at least one red) = 1 − 0.7² = 0.51; dividing gives 0.09/0.51 ≈ 17.6%, rounded to 18%.
fields.reason: The products and complement are correct: P(RR)=0.3^2=0.09; P(at least one R)=1-0.7^2=0.51; their ratio is 3/17, about 17.647%, rounded to 18%.

fields.exact_text: 9% is the unconditional probability of two red draws and ignores the restriction imposed by the condition 'at least one red.'
fields.reason: Correctly identifies 9% as the unconditional both-red probability and distinguishes it from the probability after conditioning.

fields.exact_text: 30% is the single-draw probability of red and does not correspond to any relevant probability for two draws under this conditioning event.

complete_teaching.yield_scope: Same conventional model allowed by the prospective marble anchor; the 30% relevance clause is broader than necessary but does not establish a material error in the requested conditional-event explanation. Main alone is useful but omits intermediate products/complement.

choices: Satisfied customers may be more likely to respond than dissatisfied ones
The sample size of 2,000 is too small

independent_key.warranted_exact_choice: Satisfied customers may be more likely to respond than dissatisfied ones
independent_key.scope: Unique best-listed possible concern about generalizing to all purchasers; the literal 80% among respondents can be correct.
independent_key.proof: There can be 1,600 satisfied respondents. Depending on the 8,000 nonrespondents, overall satisfaction can range from 16% to 96%. If 6,400 nonrespondents are satisfied, total satisfaction is exactly 80%, so nonresponse need not produce bias.

items.goal_fit: Relevant introductory concern about evidence and sample representativeness.

independent_difficulty.reason: Direct recognition of a familiar selection-bias concern; two sweeping or elementary-impossibility distractors make the answer easy to identify.

distractors.choice: The sample size of 2,000 is too small
distractors.reason: Confuses representativeness with size; no required precision makes 2,000 inherently too small.
A sweeping universal claim rather than a plausible competing account of this sampling process.
Simple percentage arithmetic immediately refutes it.

fields.exact_text: An 80% response rate among only 20% of recipients creates strong non-response bias: respondents systematically differ from non-respondents, inflating the reported satisfaction figure beyond the true population value.
fields.reason: The 80% is a satisfaction proportion among respondents, not the response rate; the response rate is 2,000/10,000=20%. That is a definite quantity-label error. The rest additionally claims established strong nonresponse bias, systematic differences and upward inflation beyond the true population value. None follows from the stated data. The same observation permits overall satisfaction 16%, 80% or 96%, so the sign and existence of population distortion are not established. This refutes the inference, not the possibility of bias in some unspecified actual company.

fields.choice: Satisfied customers may be more likely to respond than dissatisfied ones
fields.exact_text: Self-selection among the 20% who replied likely skews results upward, making the 80% figure unrepresentative of all 10,000 customers.
fields.reason: The option cautiously says may. Its explanation instead asserts that selection likely skews upward and makes the result unrepresentative. Neither response motives, direction, likelihood nor actual bias follows from a 20% response rate. The observed data permit an unbiased 80% population, lower satisfaction, or higher satisfaction.

fields.choice: The sample size of 2,000 is too small
fields.exact_text: 2,000 respondents yields a margin of error under ±2%, which is statistically adequate for estimating a proportion.
fields.reason: A count of 2,000 voluntary respondents alone does not establish a margin of error below two percentage points. Confidence level, sampling design/dependence and a probability-selection model are absent; sampling error does not bound selective-response bias. An under-2% interval can arise under additional conventional simple-random-sampling assumptions, so this is an unsupported unconditional precision claim, not proof that every possible specified interval exceeds 2%. Required precision is also unstated, so statistically adequate is not universal.

fields.exact_text: Email surveys are not inherently unreliable; this is too broad and fails to identify the specific, traceable bias present in this scenario.
fields.reason: It is correct that email surveys are not inherently unreliable. However, specific, traceable bias present in this scenario strengthens a possible selection mechanism into established bias. The stem establishes nonresponse and an opportunity for bias, not that respondents actually differ in satisfaction.

fields.exact_text: 80% of 2,000 respondents equals 1,600 satisfied customers, which is entirely mathematically possible.
fields.reason: 80% of 2,000 is exactly 1,600. That respondent count is possible within 10,000 invitees, so the claimed mathematical impossibility is correctly refuted.
